blocks.text: When choosing a fuel for an application, two key quantities are considered: energy density and specific energy.

blocks.title: Energy density
blocks.text: Energy density is the energy capacity of a substance, generally expressed as the quantity of energy that can be stored per unit volume of a fuel, typically in megajoules per litre (MJ/L).

Fuels with a high energy density store a large amount of energy in a relatively small volume. The book notes their use in stationary applications and storage, such as power plants and generators. For example, diesel (about 35.8 MJ/L) has a higher energy density than gasoline (about 34.2 MJ/L): it contains more energy per litre.

blocks.title: Specific energy
blocks.text: Specific energy is the amount of energy contained in a unit mass of a substance. It is typically measured in megajoules per kilogram (MJ/kg).

Specific energy matters when weight is critical, as in aircraft and spacecraft. A fuel with a high specific energy gives a lot of energy without adding much mass. For example, hydrogen gas has an extremely high specific energy (120 MJ/kg), which makes it interesting for aerospace, although its energy density is low.

blocks.title: Interesting information: CNG
blocks.text: Compressed natural gas (CNG) used in transport in Pakistan is very economical, but it has a lower energy density than petrol, so vehicles must carry a larger storage volume for enough fuel. That is why CNG suits local commuting and is not ideal for long journeys.

blocks.alt: Left: a bar chart of energy per litre: diesel about 35.8 MJ/L and gasoline about 34.2 MJ/L. Right: hydrogen gas about 120 MJ/kg, a very high specific energy useful where weight matters but with low energy density; CNG has a lower energy density than petrol, shown by a small petrol tank beside a much larger CNG cylinder (sketch, not to scale).
blocks.caption: Energy density and specific energy (original diagram for topic 31.7).
blocks.long_description: Energy density compares fuels by volume (how big the tank must be); specific energy compares them by mass (how heavy the fuel is). A fuel can be good on one measure and poor on the other, as hydrogen is.

blocks.prompt: About how much energy is stored in a 50 L tank of diesel, and in 50 L of gasoline?
blocks.explanation: Diesel: 50 x 35.8 = about 1790 MJ; gasoline: 50 x 34.2 = about 1710 MJ.

blocks.prompt: For a spacecraft, would you look for a fuel with a high energy density or a high specific energy? Why?
blocks.explanation: A high specific energy, because weight is critical: the fuel should give a lot of energy without adding much mass.

items: Energy density: energy per volume (MJ/L); diesel 35.8 > gasoline 34.2.
Specific energy: energy per mass (MJ/kg); hydrogen 120.
CNG: lower energy density, suits local commuting.
